summary: Ahmed Menshawy's talk covers three themes: the shift from structured-data AI to LLMs using unstructured data, intelligence augmentation vs. AGI hype, and challenges with technical debt in LLM deployment. Over the past 10-15 years, AI value derived from structured data via supervised and deep learning, but over 80% of organizational data is unstructured, with 71% of organizations struggling to manage and secure it. LLMs enable contextualizing this data as extended memory. Menshawy counters AGI doomsday rhetoric, recommending a Nature article urging focus on present-day AI risks rather than speculative future ones. He references LeCun's critique that LLMs are 'dumb at the core' due to autoregressive token generation where mistakes amplify, and cites Ada Lovelace's 1843 observation that machines cannot originate anything. ChatGPT's breakthrough was the natural-language user interface, enabled by outsourced manual question-response pairs. At Mastercard, LLMs boosted fraud detection by 300%. For GenAI applications, essentials include foundation model access, customization environments, build/deploy tools, and scalable infrastructure. Citing a 2015 NIPS paper, ML code is under 5% of end-to-end pipelines; surrounding infrastructure around LLM code accounts for over 90% of building such applications. Two deployment approaches exist: using foundation models as-is or with fine-tuning, which suffers from hallucination, poor attribution, staleness, revision difficulties, and limited customization. RAG addresses these by coupling the model with external memory. However, mainstream RAG treats retriever and generator as separate brains, whereas FAIR's original RAG paper trains them jointly. Menshawy highlights enterprise access control preservation as a critical challenge—organizations need specialized models for specific tasks rather than a single global LLM with access to all data. Mastercard adopted seven core principles for responsible AI covering privacy, security, and reliability, enforced by a governing body. A paper reviewer questioned whether LLMs are the right tool given the extensive challenges, but Menshawy argues transformative technology inevitably brings challenges, quoting 'you can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs.'

sections.title: From Structured to Unstructured Data and the AGI Hype
sections.summary: Menshawy outlines how AI value over 10-15 years came from structured data but 80%+ of organizational data is unstructured. LLMs enable contextualizing this data. He frames generative AI as augmenting human productivity, not AGI, and recommends focusing on current AI risks rather than speculative doomsday, citing a Nature article and noting some doomsday proponents themselves deploy risky systems.

sections.title: Algorithmic Foundations: LeCun, Lovelace, and the Autoregressive Limitation
sections.summary: References LeCun's critique that LLMs are 'dumb at the core' due to autoregressive token generation where mistakes amplify. Cites Ada Lovelace's 1843 statement that machines cannot originate anything, arguing current algorithmic foundations won't reach AGI despite transformative applications.

sections.title: ChatGPT's Real Breakthrough and Mastercard's Use Case
sections.summary: Clarifies that next-token prediction is decades old, not OpenAI's invention. ChatGPT's breakthrough was the natural-language user interface, enabled by outsourced manual question-response pairs. Announces Mastercard's 300% fraud detection improvement using LLMs, de-risked responsibly.

sections.title: Essentials for GenAI Applications and the 5% ML Code Problem
sections.summary: Four essentials: foundation model access (least challenging), customization environments (somewhat challenging), build/deploy tools (most challenging, none pre-existed LLMs), and scalable infrastructure (inference compute now exceeds training). Cites 2015 NIPS paper showing ML code is under 5% of end-to-end pipelines, redefining AI engineering scope.

sections.title: Deployment Approaches: Foundation Models vs. RAG and the Paper Introduction
sections.summary: Contrasts using foundation models as-is (suffering hallucination, attribution, staleness, revision, and customization issues) with RAG, which couples models to external memory for grounding, up-to-date information, attribution, and revision. Notes mainstream RAG separates retriever and generator while FAIR's original paper trains them jointly. Introduces his ACM EuroMLSys paper.

sections.title: End-to-End LLM Challenges, Access Controls, and Responsible AI Principles
sections.summary: Emphasizes that surrounding infrastructure around LLM code accounts for over 90% of end-to-end LLM application building. Highlights enterprise access control preservation as a critical challenge—organizations need specialized models for specific tasks rather than a global LLM with access to all data. Details Mastercard's seven core principles for responsible AI (privacy, security, reliability) enforced by a governing body. Notes a reviewer questioned whether LLMs are the right tool given the extensive challenges, but Menshawy argues transformative technology inevitably brings challenges, quoting 'you can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs.' Closes by inviting attendees to explore Mastercard's AI engineering team work.
